item.title: Mecca Agreement: A Muslim Nato or yet another Baghdad Pact?. [ middleeasteye ]
item.description:
Mecca Agreement: A Muslim Nato or yet another Baghdad Pact?

Submitted by Joseph Massad on Fri, 08/21/2026 - 21:54
The Saudi-Turkish-Pakistani pact reinforces the US-run regional order that analysts claim it defies - which explains why Trump was so quick to bless it
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif after signing a joint defence agreement in Mecca, Saudi Arabia, on 7 August 2026 (Murat Cetinmuhurdar/Turkish Presidential Press Office/Handout via Reuters)
Off

The recent Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, has reinvigorated longstanding US ambitions for a subcontracted "Middle Eastern", "Arab" or "Muslim" Nato to serve US regional security interests.

Some pro-American and pro-Israeli analysts have misconstrued the agreement as an alliance against Israel, while others see it as a sign that the Saudis are seeking new security guarantors in light of US failures to fully protect the kingdom and its Arab neighbours.

The Mecca Agreement, however, is merely the latest iteration of a US policy dating back to early in the Cold War to preserve existing pro-western regimes, their US sponsor, and their unspoken ally, Israel.

Its real targets, unsurprisingly, are the enemies of the US and Israel.

US President Donald Trump welcomed the agreement at once, declaring himself "very happy" that the three countries had "recently, and finally, signed" it.

The new agreement follows the model of the US-sponsored 1955 Central Treaty Organization (Cento), better known as the Baghdad Pact.

Pactomania

It was John Foster Dulles, secretary of state under President Dwight Eisenhower, known for his global "pactomania", who created the Baghdad Pact as the main anti-Soviet front in the Middle East. Its members included Britain, Turkey, the shah's Iran, Pakistan and Hashemite Iraq.

The Americans worked hard to enlist Jordan but failed amid nationalist anti-imperialist opposition to King Hussein's wishes. Nasser's Egypt also rejected the pact, as did then anti-Hashemite Saudi Arabia.

Joseph Massad
Read More »

The pact preceded the January 1957 articulation of the Eisenhower Doctrine, which provided the framework for American imperialist aggression aimed at protecting what the US president called "free" nations from Soviet and communist subversion.

Eisenhower insisted: "The Middle East is the birthplace of three great religions - Moslem, Christian and Hebrew. Mecca and Jerusalem are more than places on the map. They symbolize religions which teach that the spirit has supremacy over matter and that the individual has a dignity and rights of which no despotic government can rightfully deprive him. It would be intolerable if the holy places of the Middle East should be subjected to a rule that glorifies atheistic materialism."

At the time, East Jerusalem was part of Jordan, which had annexed it in 1950.

Since then, and thanks to US policies advancing Eisenhower's strategy, Mecca and Israeli-occupied and -annexed Jerusalem, it seems, have been subjected to capitalist theistic materialism rather than to the "atheistic" variety.

Despite Iraq's withdrawal after the 1958 revolution, the Baghdad Pact survived for another two decades and was dissolved only after revolutionary Iran withdrew from it in 1979, depriving the US-backed alliance of its central regional link.

Nevertheless, the US never gave up on creating a regional "Nato". In 2006-2007, US Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice hoped that the "new Middle East" to which she, on behalf of the US, wanted to give birth would include a US-led military alliance. At the time, Rice recruited Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Jordan to her new pact, but the time was not yet ripe to include Israel fully and openly.

Nato redux

The project of including Israel had to wait until 2022, when the US shepherded an Arab military alliance with Israel targeting Iran. Dubbed by some a "Middle East Nato", the Middle East Air Defense Alliance (MEAD) was unveiled by Benny Gantz, then Israel's defence minister.

Soon after, Jordan's King Abdullah announced on US television that he "would be one of the first people that would endorse a Middle East Nato", adding: "I'd like to see more countries in the area come into that mix."

At the time, this military alliance targeted Iran, Assad's Syria, Hezbollah and Hamas, and even Russia. Formal arrangements culminated in full integration within the US Central Command (Centcom) in January 2026 - on the eve of US-Israeli aggression against Iran.

A few days before the Mecca Agreement was announced, Saudi Arabia created yet another military alliance on 30 July with 13 other countries

A few days before the Mecca Agreement was announced, Saudi Arabia created yet another military alliance on 30 July with 13 other countries: Bahrain, Bangladesh, the Comoros, Djibouti, Egypt, Jordan, Kuwait, Pakistan, Qatar, Somalia, Sudan, Turkey and the Saudi-backed Aden-based Yemeni government.

The Multinational Maritime Defense Alliance (MMDA) was concluded in Riyadh to secure shipping and energy routes in the Red Sea, Bab al-Mandeb Strait and Gulf of Aden following naval blockade threats and attacks by Yemen's Ansar Allah (Houthi) movement.

The MMDA is clearly nothing but the successor to "Operation Prosperity Guardian", the American-led military campaign launched in December 2023 to punish Ansar Allah for targeting Israel-linked shipping in solidarity with Palestinians facing genocide in Gaza.

The operation included 20 nations, but Bahrain was its sole regional participant, with neighbouring states standing back for fear of being implicated or exposed as supporting Israel's genocide.

The new MMDA averts any such misapprehension by targeting Ansar Allah for its interdiction of Saudi, rather than Israeli, shipping.

Why, then, have Egypt and Jordan - two staunch US allies - not also joined the new Mecca pact?

While Egypt is reportedly still weighing its options, perhaps the absence of both countries indicates that the current signatories fear that they could be called on to intervene if either Egypt or Jordan faced an Israeli invasion or aggression, a prospect that, given Tel Aviv's relentless bellicosity and continuing threats to both countries, is not altogether unlikely.

Complement, not alternative

Some pro-Israel analysts, for their part, fear that the new agreement undermines Israel and its recent Abraham Accords partners who were not invited to join.

Council on Foreign Relations fellow Steven A Cook claims simplistically that "Trump's apparent impulsiveness has now left some in the region to wonder whether they will be left in the lurch to face an empowered Iran on their own".

He also worries that "the Saudis, who have clearly become concerned about the reliability of the United States, are now looking for other options" and that "their new security partners are seeking a new order that allows them, not Washington, to shape the region".

Why the Mecca Agreement has given the UAE-Israel alliance the jitters
Read More »

The faulty assumption here is that an alliance among three longtime US military allies - with Turkey itself a Nato member - could somehow operate independently of US authority, or that its members could act without orders from Washington.

The pro-Israel Cook concludes that "the US-aligned regional order could now become a Middle East with two blocs: the countries that remained committed to the Abraham Accords and its alternative, the Mecca Agreement".

Yet the Mecca Agreement is not an alternative to the Abraham Accords; it is a complement. After all, Turkey maintains diplomatic and trade relations with Israel, and Saudi Arabia has held unofficial talks with Tel Aviv for years and has officially sought to integrate Israel into the region since at least 1981.

Saudi Arabia is neither considered an enemy of Israel nor considers Israel its enemy. Pakistan would like to align with Israel were Israel not a major ally of its archenemy, India.

Others, such as Khalid al-Jaber, executive director of the Doha-based Middle East Council on Global Affairs, see the new agreement as a warning that "diminished American weight could leave the region inside an order whose rules are set by two actors alone: Israel and Iran".

Jaber argues that "the Mecca pact is best understood as an early attempt to build a third pole - a bloc that does not need to fight either power, but one that has enough weight to deny either a monopoly over the region".

But this interpretation is mistaken. Only last November, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman was in Washington signing a strategic defence agreement with the US, coming away a "major non-Nato ally" with a promise of F-35 jets.

Saudi Arabia is neither considered an enemy of Israel nor considers Israel its enemy

Turkey remains a Nato member, and Pakistan's prime minister thanked Trump for his "courageous and decisive leadership" within hours of his post. Indeed, there is no third pole at all.

The Mecca Agreement, like the MMDA, is an element of an updated Baghdad Pact. It joins a succession of US-organised military alliances meant to safeguard US domination of the region.

Their principal goal remains to challenge all of Israel's enemies in loyal service to US and Israeli power.

This is hardly anything new. No wonder Trump extended his congratulations to all three signatories: "Big, bold, and important first step." Enough said.

Healing through memory against terrorism. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The United Nations observes August 21 as the International Day of Remembrance of and Tribute to the Victims of Terrorism.
The 2026 theme - “Healing Through Memory” - is a particularly powerful reminder that confronting terrorism is not only about security; it is about acknowledging pain, honouring victims, and ensuring that societies heal by remembering rather than forgetting.
For Bangladesh, this day carries deep emotional weight, for our collective memory includes tragedies that reshaped the nation’s understanding of extremism. The Holey Artisan attack of July 1, 2016 remains the most devastating example in our recent history.
Yet, Holey Artisan was not an isolated wound. Operations against extremist networks over the years have revealed how militancy attempted to embed itself across the country, and it continues to be an issue to this day in some capacity.
This year’s theme therefore urges us to recognize that healing requires remembering. Survivors and families deserve acknowledgment, support, and a national commitment to ensuring their suffering is not erased.
We must remember; memory is not a burden but a safeguard. When societies remember, they remain vigilant. When they forget, they become vulnerable.
Crucially, healing also requires unity as terrorism does not distinguish between political parties or ideologies. It targets society as a whole.
As such, Bangladesh cannot afford to let partisan divides weaken our collective resolve. Countering extremism must remain a shared national priority, one that brings all political actors regardless of affiliation, civil society, religious leaders, and security agencies together rather than driving them apart.
On this day, we must honour every life lost to terrorism and militancy. Healing through memory means carrying their stories forward, learning from them, and standing united to ensure such tragedies become a topic of the past.

item.title: Vaccination saves lives. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The launch of a cholera vaccination campaign targeting 5.17 million people in 14 high-risk upazilas across Bangladesh is a timely and necessary intervention that underscores a broader truth about public health: Vaccines save lives, prevent outbreaks, and strengthen national resilience.
We are a country where waterborne diseases remain a persistent threat. As such, identifying high-risk areas and taking prompt action to vaccinate the population is, beyond simply being good policy, essential for protecting millions of Bangladeshi citizens.
Cholera is preventable, yet it continues to affect vulnerable communities, especially those living in areas with inadequate sanitation. When outbreaks occur, they not only disrupt livelihoods, but also endanger children and the elderly most.
A timely vaccination campaign is therefore our best defense against diseases such as cholera. However, the significance of this campaign therefore goes beyond cholera and reflects the importance of vaccination as a cornerstone of national health security.
Bangladesh has seen the consequences of delayed or uneven immunization - with the present measles crisis a heartbreaking reminder of these repercussions.
When vaccines are administered proactively, the entire health system benefits: Fewer hospital admissions, lower treatment costs, and stronger community resilience.
When people see the government respond quickly, transparently, and effectively, confidence in public health institutions grows. This trust is crucial for future campaigns.
The cholera campaign is a positive step and one that demonstrates what proactive health policy looks like. Our path to a healthier future however depends on ensuring that timely vaccination is the norm, not the exception. Preventing disease before it spreads is the most efficient way to curb the disease and the foundation of a more resilient, thriving nation.

US judge strikes down policy suspending immigrant visa processing for 75 nations, including Pakistan. [ dawn ]
item.description:
A US judge on Friday struck down a Trump administration policy suspending the issuance of immigrant visas to applicants from 75 countries, including Pakistan, saying that the policy exceeded Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s statutory authority.

US District Judge Jeannette Vargas in Manhattan said the policy that the State Department announced in January was “patently unlawful” and ran afoul of federal immigration law, which explicitly stripped the secretary of state of authority over consular officers’ processing of immigrant visas.

“The policy, which categorically prohibits the issuance of immigrant visas based upon the nationality of the applicant, represents a direct abrogation of this statutory scheme,” she wrote.

The State Department’s suspension that also took effect in January impacted applicants from Latin American countries including Brazil, Colombia, and Uruguay; Balkan nations such as Bosnia and Albania; South Asian countries Pakistan and Bangladesh; and those from many nations in Africa, the Middle East, and the Caribbean.

The State Department said applicants from those countries were “at a high risk for becoming a public charge and recourse to local, state and federal government resources in the United States”.

The department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the ruling.

Vargas, an appointee of Democratic former President Joe Biden, issued the ruling in a lawsuit filed by immigrant rights groups Catholic Legal Immigration Network and African Communities Together along with applicants for immigrant visas and US citizens who are sponsoring family members from the designated countries for immigrant visas.

US President Donald Trump has pursued an aggressive immigration crackdown that he says is aimed at improving domestic security.

Rights groups ⁠say ​the crackdown has violated free speech and due ​process rights and has created an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities, who have raised ​concerns about racial profiling.

item.title: No decision yet on Bangladesh PM’s visit to India, Dhaka says. [ dawn ]
item.description:
NEW DELHI: Bangladesh has not made a decision yet on Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s visit to India, his press secretary said on Friday, after Indian media reported that Rahman would be visiting New Delhi from Aug 23 to 25.

The neighbours have been in talks for weeks regarding Rahman’s first trip to New Delhi since taking office in February, as they work to repair ties strained by the 2024 ouster of Bangladesh’s former prime minister Sheikh Hasina.

She fled to India after student-led protests ended her long rule and has lived there in exile. Dhaka has repeatedly asked New Delhi to extradite her. India has said that it is examining the request.

“No decision has yet been made on the visit,” Rahman’s press secretary A. M. Saleh said, adding that Dhaka was waiting for India’s response on the extradition of Hasina and “other fugitive criminals”.

The Indian foreign ministry did not have any comments to make on the visit, spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal told reporters at a regular media briefing.

Tarique Rahman’s six-month-old government has sought to maintain good relations with India since coming to power, but signalled last week that a more favourable diplomatic environment was needed for the trip, days after Hasina addressed journalists in a move condemned by Dhaka.

Published in Dawn, August 22nd, 2026

Meezan Bank bags its 5th ‘Best Bank’ award. [ dawn ]
item.description:
• Bank of Punjab wins three awards; HBL wins ESG award
• SBP chief calls for faster banking digitisation, higher private sector credit

KARACHI: Meezan Bank Ltd was named Pakistan’s best bank for the fifth time at the 11th Pakistan Banking Awards held in Karachi on Friday, while Bank of Punjab secured honours in three categories.

Jury Chairperson Zubyr Soomro, explaining the challenges involved in selecting winners among banks and non-bank institutions, said the jury was not yet ready to announce a winner in the Best Bank category.

Subsequently, Meezan Bank secured the top award, and was also named the best bank for customer engagement. Bank of Punjab won three awards for Best Bank for Women’s Inclusion, Best SME Bank and Best Bank for Agriculture Inclusion.

In a surprise announcement during the ceremony, Bank of Punjab President and CEO Zafar Masud said the bank would not submit entries in any category next year, saying other banks should also get an opportunity to win.

Habib Bank Ltd received the award for Best Bank for Enviro­nmental, Social and Governance (ESG), while Bank Alfalah won the Digital Excellence Award.

Faysal Bank Ltd and Askari Bank were jointly named the Best Mid-Sized Bank.

The award for Best Contribution by a Non-Bank Entity went to Pakistan Microfinance Investment Company Ltd, while ASA Micr­ofinance Bank Ltd was named the Best Micro­finance Bank.

Earlier, State Bank of Pakistan Governor Jameel Ahmad spoke about the prevailing economic environment and challenges arising from the regional conflict.

He said the situation remained encouraging for banks, but private-sector credit penetration was still low and is 50 per cent compared to Bangladesh.

The governor expressed confidence that banks could help improve the situation as the government’s financing needs declined.

He also stressed the need to accelerate digitisation across the banking sector.

The 11th Pakistan Banking Awards were jointly organised by the National Institute of Banking and Finance Pakistan, A.F. Ferguson & Co and Dawn Media Group.

Published in Dawn, August 22nd, 2026

item.title: Helping the youth help the nation. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The call for Bangladesh’s youth to pursue skill development with national interests in mind is both timely and necessary.
As the country faces a rapidly changing global economy, technological disruption, and an increasingly competitive international labour market, young people cannot afford to remain confined to conventional career paths.
Their skills must, therefore, be relevant to emerging industries, changing market demands, and the broader needs of the economy.
However, the responsibility for building a productive, skilled, and socially conscious youth population cannot rest on young people alone.
If the state expects the youth to work for the national interest, then the nation and the state must reciprocate by creating an environment in which young people can actually realize their potential.
As the minister rightly pointed out, training people for existing jobs is insufficient; Bangladesh must also create new employment opportunities and expand the market itself.
This requires coherent industrial policies, investment in emerging sectors, easier access to finance for entrepreneurs, stronger infrastructure, and an education and training system that responds to actual market needs.
Most importantly, skills development must lead somewhere; it is unfair to repeatedly urge young people to become more employable when decent employment remains scarce, wages fail to reflect skills, and opportunities are concentrated in a limited number of sectors.
A skilled generation without adequate avenues to apply those skills represents not only individual frustration but also a significant loss of national potential.
The example of policy support that helped lay the foundations of Bangladesh’s garment industry demonstrates what can happen when human capital development is matched with appropriate state intervention.
Our youth should certainly recognize their responsibility to the country, but the country must also recognize its responsibility to them.
Bangladesh’s young people are among its most valuable drivers. If we expect them to build the nation, we must give them the tools, opportunities, and institutional support to do so.

Redefining the president’s role. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh welcomes Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir as its new president. Congratulations are in order for a man who fully deserves this honour after decades of public service.
His election -- the first genuinely contested presidential vote in decades -- marks an important democratic moment for our country as we continue to try and bring back democratic ideals that were all but lost in our recent history.
With that said, we must remember that Mirza Fakhrul now assumes the nation’s highest constitutional office and thus, invites a necessary conversation about what the presidency has been in Bangladesh, and what it could become.
For much of this country’s history, the presidency has been treated as largely ceremonial. Indeed, that the president has been confined to formal duties such as issuing messages, attending state functions, and performing the rituals of office is not all a president of a nation should be reduced to.
This is a role that carries immense symbolic weight, being the only office meant to stand above partisanship and representing the republic rather than any single political interest. This is key for a nation that looks to have only become more politically polarized over the years.
Bangladesh today faces institutional challenges that demand steady national leadership. The presidency can -- and should -- play a more meaningful part in shaping our democratic culture.
Given Mirza Fakhrul’s long history in politics and his involvement with Bangladesh ever since its inception, he has the pedigree to speak when others cannot, urge restraint when tensions rise, and elevate issues that require long‑term national attention.
The question now is whether he will be empowered and encouraged to do so. Bangladesh, however, would benefit from a president who is more active in its nation-building endeavours.
President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir now has the opportunity to redefine expectations. We congratulate him, and hope his role is allowed to be not just ceremonial, but genuinely impactful for the betterment of our nation.

item.title: A warning we cannot afford to ignore. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The Secondary School Certificate (SSC) examination has long been regarded as a major academic milestone in Bangladesh -- a high-stakes examination that shapes students' academic and career prospects. Yet, the high failure rate in this year's SSC results has raised serious concerns among educators, families, and policy-makers.
The poor performance in core subjects, particularly English and Mathematics, is troubling. It might be tempting to dismiss the results as an isolated setback or a sign of declining student capability, but doing so would be a mistake.
Instead, these outcomes should be recognized as a warning sign of systemic weaknesses within our education system.
If Bangladesh is serious about building the human capital required for a competitive, technology-driven economy, it must look past mere examination results and confront the roots of learning deficits. The core issue is not simply why so many students failed this year, but why the education system has allowed them to reach the SSC level without acquiring the essential knowledge and competencies for success.
The SSC crisis reflects unaddressed learning gaps originating in primary school and widening through secondary education. Burdened by a high-stress curriculum, students with foundational weaknesses in core subjects -- such as English, math, and analytical reasoning -- inevitably struggle as coursework grows more complex.
Without early intervention, the system advances students who lack basic competencies. Viewed in this light, an SSC failure is not a sudden mishap, but the visible symptom of a multi-year learning deficit.
For decades, much of our education system has placed excessive emphasis on rote memorization, examination scores, and GPA-5s rather than genuine comprehension. Students are encouraged to reproduce textbook material instead of analyzing, questioning, applying, and problem-solving.
This approach has fostered a dependence on guidebooks, model answers, and strictly examination-oriented preparation. Consequently, when assessments demand conceptual understanding rather than predictable recall, many students struggle.
The core issue is not simply that students cannot answer difficult questions; it is that the system has consistently failed to teach them how to think critically.
Schools are not just places for learning from textbooks. They are also important centers for children’s physical, mental, social, and moral development.
At the primary level, children need to develop essential life skills such as social interaction, emotional control, communication, creativity, and cooperation. At the secondary level, these should be strengthened with skills such as problem-solving, critical thinking, effective communication, digital literacy, and leadership.
The goal of education, therefore, should not be limited to getting good marks in examinations; it should also prepare students for life and the world of work.
Compounding this is the systemic concern surrounding fairness and transparency in teacher recruitment. Because teachers play a vital role in properly guiding students during their foundational years, addressing deployment policies and continuous professional development remains an urgent priority.
Many institutions, particularly outside major urban centers, face severe shortages of qualified educators in critical subjects. However, merely recruiting qualified teachers is insufficient.
To foster a thriving learning environment, educators also require ongoing professional development, meaningful evaluation frameworks, and robust career support.
Education reform must therefore address the entire teacher life-cycle -- from recruitment and induction to training and professional accountability.
Another neglected issue is the disruption of academic activities in schools. Political unrest, student conflicts, institutional disputes, and administrative challenges frequently reduce instructional time while undermining attendance and learning continuity.
Educational institutions must remain sanctuaries for learning, intellectual development, and academic freedom. To achieve this, the government and political parties must forge a consensus to keep schools and universities entirely free from organized partisan politics and political interference.
A substantial disparity persists between well-resourced institutions in major cities and schools in rural or disadvantaged areas. While urban institutions typically enjoy access to qualified teachers, modern laboratories, and digital infrastructure, rural institutions often struggle with chronic teacher shortages and inadequate facilities.
Consequently, public investment must prioritize institutions where educational resources are weakest.
The proliferation of coaching centers and private tutoring is both a symptom and a consequence of systemic weaknesses in mainstream education. When students and parents lose faith in classroom instruction, they naturally turn to external alternatives.
However, commercial coaching prioritizes exam-oriented tactics over true comprehension. Moreover, excessive reliance on private tutoring exacerbates inequality, as affluent families can easily afford supplemental academic support.
Ultimately, the definitive solution lies in restoring public confidence in mainstream classroom teaching.
Education policy should transcend shifting political cycles. Bangladesh requires a stable, long-term national framework rooted in evidence and broad consultation.
To achieve this, a permanent, independent National Education Commission -- comprising educators, researchers, and stakeholders -- should be established to periodically review curricula, assessments, and teacher development.
A core mandate of the Commission should be steering the education system toward outcome- or competency-based education (OBE/CBE) from primary school to higher education. By drawing on successful regional models, such as India’s National Education Policy 2020 and reforms in Malaysia, Bangladesh can align its teaching and assessment standards with clear, measurable competencies suited to its own context.
Assessment must measure whether students have mastered expected competencies rather than merely testing their capacity to reproduce memorized material.
Policy-makers and educators must prioritize conceptual understanding, analytical ability, problem-solving, effective communication, and the practical application of knowledge. While continuous or school-based assessment can play a valuable role, it requires robust moderation and rigorous quality assurance to prevent grade inflation.
Recent SSC results serve as a stark reminder that educational quality cannot be measured by pass rates alone. A high pass rate does not guarantee meaningful learning, just as a low pass rate does not place the blame for poor performance solely on students.
While Bangladesh has made remarkable progress in expanding educational access, the next critical challenge is ensuring true comprehension -- cultivating young people equipped to think critically, solve problems, communicate effectively, and leverage technology intelligently.
Consequently, these results should not be dismissed as an isolated setback, but rather seized as an opportunity to confront systemic weaknesses and enact lasting reforms.
MM Shahidul Hassan is a distinguished professor at Eastern University, and former Vice Chancellor of East West University, Bangladesh.

item.title: When hope travels, so does exploitation. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
"I crossed the border without documents or a passport. A friend I met through social media promised me a better-paying job at a beauty parlour. I believed I was chasing a better future. Instead, I was sexually exploited and eventually ended up in jail."
She shared these words with me shortly after she was repatriated to Dhaka.
What stayed with me was not only her story, but also the question she asked before we parted.
"If someone had told me what could happen, would my life have been different?"
I have returned to that question many times since.
Over the years, through my work with returnee migrants and survivors of trafficking and exploitative migration, I have listened to many stories of journeys that ended very differently from how they began.
Yet the experiences of women have stayed with me the most. Their stories are not simply about migration gone wrong. They reveal how hope can become a pathway to exploitation when it is shaped by misinformation, unequal power, and limited choices.
Months later, I met another woman whose story unsettled me in a different way. She had travelled to Saudi Arabia believing she had secured a job as a domestic worker. Instead, she was subjected to repeated sexual violence. Even the person she trusted to help her escape exploited her further.
When she eventually returned to Bangladesh, she was pregnant as a result of that abuse. Yet what struck me was not only the violence she endured abroad, but also what awaited her at home. Instead of finding comfort, she found silence and rejection. Her family struggled to accept both her and her child.
The two women had never met. Their journeys followed different routes and ended in different countries. Yet their stories began in remarkably similar ways.
Someone they trusted promised them a better future.
Listening to these women changed how I understand labour migration. Before meeting them, I often thought about trafficking and labour exploitation as crimes committed by traffickers or abusive employers. Their stories challenged that assumption.
Neither woman intended to become an irregular migrant or a survivor of exploitation. Both believed they were making responsible decisions for themselves and their families. Their journeys began not with criminal intent, but with trust.
As I reflected on their experiences, I realized I had been asking the wrong question. I had been asking how exploitation happens. They led me to ask why so many women are placed in situations where exploitation becomes possible in the first place.
Sociologists have long argued that migration is shaped by the interaction between individual aspirations and the broader social and economic structures that shape people's choices. People migrate because opportunities at home are limited while possibilities elsewhere appear within reach.
Yet contemporary research reminds us that exploitation rarely begins with violence. It emerges where poverty, gender inequality, deceptive recruitment, limited information, and unequal power converge. By the time exploitation becomes visible, vulnerability has often been building long before a woman boards a plane or crosses a border.
The first woman did not cross the border because she wanted to take unnecessary risks. She crossed because someone convinced her the risks were small. The second woman did not leave believing she would be abused. She left believing she had secured legitimate employment.
What failed them was not simply their judgement. It was the system of trust surrounding their decisions.
That trust is easy to understand.
Across Bangladesh, labour migration has become part of many families' aspirations. A neighbour returns with a newly built house. A relative pays for a child's education through overseas earnings. A family escapes debt because someone found work abroad. These stories travel quickly through communities, quietly shaping the belief that migration is the surest path to a better life.
The stories that travel less often are those of women who return carrying trauma instead of opportunity.
Many of the women I have spoken with could clearly remember the salaries they had been promised. Few, however, knew much about their employment contracts, their rights in the destination country, or where they could seek help if something went wrong.
Some relied entirely on verbal assurances from brokers or acquaintances. Others believed paperwork could be completed after arrival. None imagined that the very people they trusted could become part of the danger.
Whenever I meet returnee migrants now, I find myself listening differently. I no longer hear only where they travelled or how they returned. I listen for the moment when hope first became vulnerability.
Women often face additional risks because many migrate into domestic work, where employment takes place inside private homes. Unlike most workplaces, these environments remain largely hidden from public oversight, making abuse, sexual violence, wage theft, and restrictions on movement far more difficult to detect or report.
When exploitation occurs, seeking help can itself become another source of vulnerability, as the second woman's experience painfully demonstrated.
Yet the challenges rarely end when women return home.
For many survivors, the violence they experienced abroad is followed by silence, stigma, and social rejection. Reintegration becomes more than finding employment again. It becomes the struggle to rebuild dignity, relationships, and a sense of belonging.
The woman I met at the border asked whether someone could have changed her future simply by telling her the truth.
The more I reflect on her question, the less I believe it is only about information.
It is about responsibility.
Families are often the first people a woman turns to before deciding to migrate. Asking difficult questions before encouraging that decision may be just as important as celebrating the opportunity itself.
Is the recruiter licensed? Has the employment contract been verified? Does she understand her rights? Does she know where to seek help if something goes wrong? These conversations may not eliminate every risk, but they can help women make informed choices.
The government has an equally important responsibility. Safer migration requires stronger oversight of recruitment practices, transparent migration processes, accessible information, gender-responsive pre-departure orientation, effective protection through Bangladeshi missions abroad, and survivor-centred reintegration that recognizes recovery as more than an economic process.
Protection should accompany women throughout the migration journey, not begin only after exploitation has occurred.
I often find myself returning to the question the first woman asked me.
"If someone had told me what could happen, would my life have been different?"
Perhaps that question should no longer belong only to her. It should belong to every family deciding whether to send a daughter abroad. It should belong to every recruiter whose promises influence life-changing decisions. It should belong to policy-makers responsible for protecting migrant workers. And it should belong to all of us who celebrate migration's economic contributions while too rarely listening to those whose journeys ended differently.
Her question cannot change the past. But it can shape the future.
If it encourages one family to ask harder questions, one woman to seek reliable information before leaving home, or one institution to strengthen protection before another journey begins, then perhaps fewer women will one day have to ask it at all.
Md Shihabul Hossain is deputy manager, migration program, Brac.

Letting our cultural heritage shine. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The transformation of Jamalpur’s nakshi kantha from a household craft into a thriving small and medium-sized industry is a welcome reminder that Bangladesh’s cultural heritage can also be a source of sustainable livelihoods.
With more than 500 women entrepreneurs now involved in the sector, the craft is creating employment, empowering women, and reaching markets both at home and abroad.
Yet the value of nakshi kantha extends far beyond its commercial success: Each embroidered design carries elements of our collective history, aesthetics and rural traditions.
These designs represent forms of artistic expression that have been passed down through generations, and preserving such traditions is therefore essential to preserving an important part of our cultural identity.
This is why the small businesses and individual artisans keeping these crafts alive deserve greater recognition and support.
In many cases, these enterprises operate from homes, allowing women to balance economic activity with household responsibilities. Their success demonstrates how heritage-based businesses can contribute to inclusive local development without requiring large-scale industrial infrastructure.
However, traditional crafts face a constant challenge: Adapting to changing consumer preferences without losing their distinctive character.
The expansion of nakshi embroidery into clothing, accessories, and home decor is encouraging, but innovation should complement tradition rather than gradually replace it.
Artisans should be supported with training in design, quality control, branding, and digital commerce so they can compete in modern markets while retaining authentic techniques and motifs.
Government agencies, cultural institutions, and private businesses should also work together to create stronger domestic and international markets for indigenous crafts.
The Geographical Indication (GI) recognition, as received by Jamalpur’s nakshi kantha in 2024, should be followed by effective branding, market access, and protection against imitation.
Ultimately, heritage survives when it remains relevant to the people who inherit it. Supporting artisans and small enterprises is, therefore, an investment in the economy as well as in keeping Bangladesh’s artistic traditions alive for future generations.

item.title: Taxes should feel like a responsibility, not a burden. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s call for a simpler, corruption-free, and people-friendly revenue system is both timely and necessary.
Bangladesh cannot build a stronger economy while relying disproportionately on the same pool of compliant taxpayers; thus expanding the tax net, rather than repeatedly increasing the burden on existing taxpayers, must become the foundation of a sustainable revenue strategy.
For too long, taxation has often been associated with complexity, uncertainty, and, at times, harassment. Such experiences naturally discourage voluntary compliance and create distrust between citizens and the revenue administration.
If paying taxes is to become a civic responsibility rather than an unpleasant obligation, the process must be made transparent, predictable, and accessible.
This requires meaningful reform within the National Board of Revenue (NBR). Digitalization and data-driven administration can help identify eligible taxpayers, reduce opportunities for discretion and corruption, and make assessment and collection more efficient.
At the same time, technology must not become another layer of bureaucracy: Systems should be designed with ordinary taxpayers and small businesses in mind, with straightforward procedures and accessible support.
Broadening the tax base also requires addressing the large informal economy. Bringing eligible individuals and businesses into the formal system should be pursued through incentives, education, and simplified compliance, rather than relying exclusively on punitive measures.
VAT administration, too, must be streamlined so that legitimate businesses are not burdened by unnecessary complexity.
Most importantly, the government must establish a culture of fairness. Those who fulfil their obligations should be treated with respect, while deliberate tax evasion should face appropriate consequences.
Revenue collection works best when citizens believe the system is equitable and that their contributions are being used responsibly.
A people-friendly tax system is also about building trust between the state and its citizens. If the government can make taxation simpler, fairer, and more transparent, stronger revenue collection can follow naturally -- and with it, so will the greater capacity to fund Bangladesh’s development.
